advances: Establishes one support-independent strict capacity-second-moment surplus for the entire class of finite complete full-rank planar lattice supports with more than four sites, uniformly over all finite tilts. Capacity factorization then supplies an exponential surplus when such planar factors are tensorized. This does not supply a support-independent source-to-row likelihood-variance bound or a depth conversion.

proof:
Extend each law by zero to all of \(\mathbb Z^2\). Use the reflected Hellinger mass from the proof of accepted fact bf1ff94487296374:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf H_{\mathbf j}(p)&
=\sum_{\mathbf x\in\mathbb Z^2}
\sqrt{p_{\mathbf x}p_{2\mathbf j-\mathbf x}},\\
s(p)&=\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}p_{\mathbf j}\mathsf H_{\mathbf j}(p),\\
v(p)&=\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}p_{\mathbf j}
\bigl(\mathsf H_{\mathbf j}(p)-s(p)\bigr)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

The scalar \(s(p)\) is exactly the scalar called \(S\) in equation (36) of that fact, not the mixed-integer set \(S\) of the locked problem. The parity identity and reflected-pair bound in equations (33)--(37) of the accepted fact give

\[
s(p)=\sum_{\mathbf c\in(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^2}\pi_{\mathbf c}^2
\ge\frac14,
\qquad
\mathcal B_2(p)\ge s(p)^2+v(p),
\tag{1}
\]

where \(\pi_{\mathbf c}\) is the mass of parity class \(\mathbf c\). We will show that no sequence in the class of the statement can satisfy \(\mathcal B_2(p_k)\to1/16\).

First establish a tail estimate that does not use log-affinity. For a finite law and a linear functional \(f\) taking distinct values on its support, pairing reflected endpoints on opposite sides of \(\mathbf j\) and applying Cauchy--Schwarz gives

\[
\mathsf H_{\mathbf j}(p)
\le p_{\mathbf j}
+2\sqrt{p\{f(\mathbf X)<f(\mathbf j)\}
\,p\{f(\mathbf X)>f(\mathbf j)\}}.
\tag{2}
\]

Indeed, the term with \(\mathbf x=\mathbf j\) is \(p_{\mathbf j}\). Each remaining reflected pair has one endpoint below and one above \(\mathbf j\), and the two orientations contribute twice the sum of the square roots of the endpoint masses. The sets of lower and upper endpoints in that sum are subsets of the two events in (2).

Suppose a strict linear halfspace contains mass at least \(\delta>0\), and every atom in it has mass at most \(t>0\). Order the support from the extreme end of this halfspace inward. A sufficiently small generic perturbation of its defining functional makes all values distinct while leaving every point of the strict halfspace before every point outside it. This is possible because the support is finite and the functional values of these two finite sets have a positive gap. Take the shortest initial segment whose mass is at least \(\delta\). It lies in the specified halfspace, has mass at most \(\delta+t\), and each of its atoms has mass at most \(t\). For every center in this segment, one of the two tail probabilities in (2) is at most \(\delta+t\). Consequently, if
\(t+2\sqrt{\delta+t}<1/8\) and \(s(p)\ge1/4\), then

\[
v(p)\ge\delta\left(\frac18\right)^2=\frac{\delta}{64}.
\tag{3}
\]

Next record the elementary planar lattice geometry needed below. If \(Q\) is a full-dimensional lattice polygon with \(M\) lattice points, then it contains a unimodular triangle with lattice vertices, and \(\operatorname{area}(Q)\le M\). Here is a proof, so no polygon classification or area formula is imported. Triangulate the polygon and insert all of its lattice points into the triangulation, splitting the containing triangle or edge at each insertion. Every resulting triangle is lattice-point-free apart from its three vertices. Such a triangle has determinant of absolute value one: translate one vertex to zero and write the other vertices as \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\). If the integer matrix with these columns had determinant of absolute value greater than one, its inverse could not be an integer matrix. For some coordinate vector, taking the fractional parts of its inverse image would therefore give a nonzero lattice point \(t\mathbf a+s\mathbf b\), with \(0\le t,s<1\). If \(t+s\le1\), this point is an additional point of the triangle; otherwise \(\mathbf a+\mathbf b-(t\mathbf a+s\mathbf b)\) is such a point. Both possibilities contradict emptiness. Thus each resulting triangle has area \(1/2\). If there are \(B\) boundary lattice points and \(I\) interior lattice points, the number of triangles is \(B+2I-2\): start with a triangulation of the original vertices, and note that inserting a boundary point adds one triangle while inserting an interior point adds two, including when the point lies on an interior edge. Therefore the area is \(I+B/2-1\le M\). This also proves the asserted existence of a unimodular triangle.

Assume for contradiction that complete full-rank supports \(D_k\), each with more than four sites, and log-affine laws \(p_k\) satisfy \(\mathcal B_2(p_k)\to1/16\). By (1),

\[
s(p_k)\longrightarrow\frac14,
\qquad v(p_k)\longrightarrow0.
\tag{4}
\]

Put \(\varepsilon=\delta_0=1/1024\). The inequality
\(\varepsilon+2\sqrt{\delta_0+\varepsilon}<1/8\) holds. For all sufficiently large \(k\), the set of atoms with mass at least \(\varepsilon\) has full affine rank two. To prove this, suppose that these atoms lie on an affine line \(L\). If there are at least two such atoms, take the line through them; if there is just one, take an integer affine line through it; if there are none, take any integer affine line. Every atom on either strict side of \(L\) has mass less than \(\varepsilon\). By (3) and \(v(p_k)<\delta_0/64\), neither side can have mass at least \(\delta_0\). Hence \(q=p_k(L)>1-2\delta_0\).

The support \(E=D_k\cap L\) of the conditional law \(p_k(\cdot\mid L)\) is complete in its intrinsic affine lattice, has rank at most one, and is log-affine. Restricting the exponential sum defining capacity to \(E\) shows, at every \(\mathbf j\in E\), that \(\mathsf C_{p_k}(\mathbf j)\ge q\mathsf C_{p_k(\cdot\mid L)}(\mathbf j)\). Accepted fact bf1ff94487296374, equation (5), therefore gives

\[
\mathcal B_2(p_k)
\ge q^3\mathcal B_2\bigl(p_k(\cdot\mid L)\bigr)
\ge\frac{q^3}{4}
>\frac{(1-2\delta_0)^3}{4}
>\frac18.
\tag{5}
\]

For a singleton conditional support the same bound follows from rank zero. Equation (5) contradicts \(\mathcal B_2(p_k)\to1/16\). The rank assertion follows, and we discard the finitely many exceptional indices.

Let \(Q_k\) be the convex hull of the atoms with mass at least \(\varepsilon\). Every lattice point of \(Q_k\) belongs to \(D_k\) by completeness, and has mass at least \(\varepsilon\) by log-affinity. Thus \(Q_k\) has at most \(1/\varepsilon\) lattice points. Choose a unimodular triangle in \(Q_k\). Apply an integer unimodular affine change of coordinates sending its vertices to \(\mathbf0,\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\). Capacity and its second moment are invariant under this change: substitute the transpose linear map in the vector over which the exponential infimum is taken. Completeness is also invariant. Continue to denote the transformed support and law by \(D_k,p_k\). We now have

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_k(\mathbf0),\ p_k(\mathbf e_1),\ p_k(\mathbf e_2)&\ge\varepsilon,\\
p_k(\mathbf x)&=a_k e^{\boldsymbol\ell_k\cdot\mathbf x}
\quad(\mathbf x\in D_k),\\
\varepsilon\le a_k\le1,&\qquad
|(\boldsymbol\ell_k)_i|\le\log(1/\varepsilon).
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]

There is a uniform spatial bound on every fixed-size atom after this normalization. For \(0<t\le\varepsilon\), form the lattice polygon
\(Q_{k,t}=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf x:p_k(\mathbf x)\ge t\}\).
It contains \(\mathbf0,\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\). All of its lattice points have mass at least \(t\), so it has at most \(1/t\) lattice points and area at most \(1/t\). For any \(\mathbf x\in Q_{k,t}\), the triangles with vertices \(\mathbf0,\mathbf e_1,\mathbf x\) and \(\mathbf0,\mathbf e_2,\mathbf x\) lie in this polygon. Their areas give

\[
p_k(\mathbf x)\ge t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
|x_1|\le2/t,\quad |x_2|\le2/t.
\tag{7}
\]

The sequence of normalized laws is tight on \(\mathbb Z^2\). In fact, fix any sufficiently small \(\delta>0\), and choose \(0<t\le\varepsilon\) so small that \(t+2\sqrt{\delta+t}<1/8\). Take an integer \(R\ge2/t\). By (7), every atom in any of the four coordinate halfspaces \(x_i>R\) or \(x_i<-R\) has mass less than \(t\). For all sufficiently large \(k\), (3) and (4) imply that each such halfspace has mass less than \(\delta\). Thus
\(p_k\bigl(\mathbb Z^2\setminus[-R,R]^2\bigr)<4\delta\).
Since \(\delta\) can be arbitrarily small, this proves tightness of the tail of the sequence.

Pass to a subsequence along which \(a_k\to a\ge\varepsilon\), \(\boldsymbol\ell_k\to\boldsymbol\ell\), and all support indicators \(\mathbf1_{D_k}(\mathbf x)\) converge for \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb Z^2\). The first two extractions use the boundedness in (6); the third uses a diagonal extraction over the countable lattice. Set
\(D_\infty=\{\mathbf x:\mathbf1_{D_k}(\mathbf x)\to1\}\).
It contains \(\mathbf0,\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\), and the pointwise limiting law is

\[
p_\infty(\mathbf x)=
\begin{cases}
a e^{\boldsymbol\ell\cdot\mathbf x},&\mathbf x\in D_\infty,\\
0,&\mathbf x\notin D_\infty.
\end{cases}
\tag{8}
\]

Tightness and pointwise convergence show that \(\sum_{\mathbf x}p_\infty(\mathbf x)=1\) and \(\|p_k-p_\infty\|_1\to0\). For completeness of this step, the mass on every finite box converges. Tightness lets such a box carry arbitrarily close to total mass uniformly for large \(k\), forcing total limiting mass one; the same boxes then bound the \(\ell^1\) difference by its vanishing finite-box part and the two small tails. Also \(D_\infty\) is complete: an integer point in its convex hull is a convex combination of finitely many of its points; these points all belong to \(D_k\) for large \(k\), so completeness puts that integer point in every sufficiently large \(D_k\), and hence in \(D_\infty\).

Reflected Hellinger masses converge uniformly in their center. Indeed, with \(f_k=\sqrt{p_k}\), \(f_\infty=\sqrt{p_\infty}\), and reflection \((R_{\mathbf j}f)(\mathbf x)=f(2\mathbf j-\mathbf x)\), we have

\[
\mathsf H_{\mathbf j}(p_k)=\langle f_k,R_{\mathbf j}f_k\rangle,
\qquad
\bigl|\mathsf H_{\mathbf j}(p_k)-\mathsf H_{\mathbf j}(p_\infty)\bigr|
\le2\|f_k-f_\infty\|_2
\le2\sqrt{\|p_k-p_\infty\|_1}.
\tag{9}
\]

For each \(\mathbf j\in D_\infty\), its limiting mass is positive. Its summand in \(v(p_k)\), together with (4) and (9), therefore gives
\(\mathsf H_{\mathbf j}(p_\infty)=1/4\).

For every summable probability law on \(\mathbb Z^2\), however, its reflected Hellinger mass tends to zero as the center tends to infinity. To see this, approximate its square root in \(\ell^2\) by a finite-support truncation \(f\). The reflected inner product of \(f\) with itself is zero once twice the center leaves the finite sumset of its support. The error in the inner product is at most twice the \(\ell^2\) approximation error, as in (9). It follows that \(D_\infty\) must be finite.

For large \(k\), every point of this finite \(D_\infty\) belongs to \(D_k\). Let \(q_k=p_k(D_\infty)\to1\) and \(\widehat p_k=p_k(\cdot\mid D_\infty)\). Restricting the capacity exponential sum, just as in (5), gives
\(\mathcal B_2(p_k)\ge q_k^3\mathcal B_2(\widehat p_k)\).
The capacities of these conditional laws converge to those of \(p_\infty\). In detail, write \(H(\nu)=-\sum_{\mathbf x}\nu_{\mathbf x}\log\nu_{\mathbf x}\), omitting zero summands. For a log-affine positive law \(p\) on the fixed finite support \(D_\infty\), the entropy formula of accepted fact bf1ff94487296374 yields

\[
\mathsf C_p(\mathbf j)=p_{\mathbf j}
\exp\!\left(\max_{\substack{\nu\text{ a law on }D_\infty\\
\sum_{\mathbf x}\nu_{\mathbf x}\mathbf x=\mathbf j}}H(\nu)\right).
\tag{10}
\]

Indeed, log-affinity and the mean constraint imply
\(D(\nu\|p)=-H(\nu)-\log p_{\mathbf j}\).
The entropy maximum in (10) depends only on the fixed support and center, not the tilt. Thus (10) proves continuity, including at boundary centers. Taking limits now gives \(\mathcal B_2(p_\infty)\le1/16\). The support \(D_\infty\) is complete and full-rank, so equations (5)--(6) of accepted fact bf1ff94487296374 force equality and show that \(D_\infty\) consists of exactly four vertices, with uniform law.

Such a complete four-vertex lattice quadrilateral is unimodularly equivalent to the unit square. To verify this classification, write its vertices in cyclic order as \(\mathbf v_0,\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_2,\mathbf v_3\). The diagonal \(\mathbf v_1\mathbf v_3\) divides it into two empty lattice triangles. The first is unimodular by the elementary triangle argument above, so transform \(\mathbf v_0,\mathbf v_1,\mathbf v_3\) to \(\mathbf0,\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\). Convexity places the remaining vertex strictly in the positive quadrant and beyond the line \(x_1+x_2=1\). The second empty triangle has determinant \(x_1+x_2-1=1\), evaluated at that vertex. Its positive integer coordinates therefore sum to two and must both be one. Apply this fixed affine unimodular change to the whole subsequence. We may now assume
\(D_\infty=\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\}\).

Finally, any complete lattice support containing these four square vertices and any additional point contains an additional point in the fixed box \(F=\{-1,0,1,2\}^2\). Here is an explicit verification. Reflect either coordinate by \(x_i\mapsto1-x_i\) if needed, and interchange the coordinates. These symmetries preserve both the square and \(F\), and put the additional point in the form \((N,M)\) with integers \(N\ge2\) and \(0\le M\le N\). If \(M=0\), the point \((2,0)\) lies on the segment from the origin to \((N,0)\). If \(M=N\), the point \((2,2)\) lies on the segment from \((1,1)\) to \((N,N)\). If \(1\le M\le N-1\) and \(N=2\), the additional point itself is \((2,1)\). In the remaining case \(N>2\), set \(\lambda=1/(N-1)\) and \(y=(N-1-M)/(N-2)\in[0,1]\). Then
\((2,1)=\lambda(N,M)+(1-\lambda)(1,y)\).
Thus in every case the convex hull contains a lattice point of \(F\) outside the square, and completeness includes that point in the support.

For all sufficiently large \(k\), the four vertices of \(D_\infty\) belong to \(D_k\), and convergence of the indicators on the finite box \(F\) gives \(D_k\cap F=D_\infty\). But \(|D_k|>4\), so the preceding verification forces an additional point in \(D_k\cap F\). This contradiction excludes every sequence with \(\mathcal B_2(p_k)\to1/16\).

The class of pairs \((D,\boldsymbol\ell)\) in the statement is nonempty, and its capacity second moments lie in \([1/16,1]\). Let \(\gamma\) be their infimum. If \(\gamma=1/16\), choosing pairs with moments tending to that infimum would produce the sequence just excluded. Hence \(\gamma>1/16\). Taking the single absolute constant \(g=16\gamma>1\) proves \(16\mathcal B_2(p)\ge g\) simultaneously for every support and every finite tilt, as required.
statement:
There exists an absolute constant \(g>1\) such that the following holds. For every finite set \(D\subseteq\mathbb Z^2\) satisfying \(D=\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^2\), \(\dim\operatorname{aff}(D)=2\), and \(|D|>4\), and every \(\boldsymbol\ell\in\mathbb R^2\), set

\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{\mathbf x}&=\frac{e^{\boldsymbol\ell\cdot\mathbf x}}{Z},
\qquad Z=\sum_{\mathbf y\in D}e^{\boldsymbol\ell\cdot\mathbf y},\\
\mathsf C_p(\mathbf j)&=\inf_{\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^2}
\sum_{\mathbf x\in D}p_{\mathbf x}e^{\mathbf u\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf j)},\\
\mathcal B_2(p)&=\sum_{\mathbf j\in D}p_{\mathbf j}\mathsf C_p(\mathbf j)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Then \(16\mathcal B_2(p)\ge g\). Here \(D\) is exactly the support denoted by \(A\) in accepted fact bf1ff94487296374, with intrinsic rank \(r=2\); the capacity and its second moment have exactly that fact's normalization. The assertion is uniform as both the polygon and the tilt vary. The proof gives existence of \(g\), not an explicit numerical value.
